1	# Outline — what the paper says and what carries it (revision 11: verdicts per claim; review #5 applied; Brief rev. 11: P6 κ* net of null cells, design-only control C3, threshold floor)
2	
3	Source: `idea-repo` Brief revision 11 (the idea, the predictions P1–P5, the study design and cell budget), the objective (`story-repo`#1) and `prior_work.md`. This page says *what to test and where it shows*, never what a result must be. Every claim below has a "refuted if" line; a result that triggers it changes the claim, and I take it to `idea-repo` (see "When results do not carry it").
4	
5	## 1. The story in one paragraph
6	Regression-adjustment estimators of the global average treatment effect (GATE) under network interference (Chin 2019; Han–Ugander 2023) fit outcome on functions of the assignment (own treatment, treated-neighbour fraction, …) and predict at all-treated and all-control. Published work shows they *can* work but gives no account of *how well, why, and when not*. We treat the estimator as **extrapolation from the observed exposure distribution to the two global corners** and ask what that predicts. The error splits into a **variance part** (OLS leverage of the corner contrast, scaling like d/(p(1−p)n)) and a **bias part** (curvature of the response × raw distance of the corner from the observed exposure support, roughly *not* growing with degree). The two parts have different drivers and, for the fraction feature, are predicted to move in opposite directions with degree (count, 2-hop and threshold mechanisms have their own predicted scalings), so "error grows with degree" is predicted to hold only where noise dominates. Abstract wording follows §3b: the bias part is *not* independent of d for (b) and (d). We test these scalings across interference mechanisms, graph families (synthetic and two real Facebook graphs), treatment probabilities and designs (Bernoulli, graph-cluster); map where regression beats and loses to difference-in-means (DM) and to exposure-mapping HT/Hájek; ask whether flexible/data-adaptive learners help; and test a data-computable two-part diagnostic against pre-registered trivial predictors (result: the variance part holds; the bias part does not, and the paper does not describe any score as a bias diagnostic). Not a new estimator: a verified, predictive account of when to trust an existing one. Positive, negative and mixed outcomes are all reported.
7	
8	## 2. Position against prior work (Related work, one paragraph per cluster)

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

Unless stated otherwise, results are for Bernoulli assignment and $\sigma=0.5$, on the synthetic graphs of Section~\ref{sec:design}; intervals are Monte Carlo intervals that treat graph draws as the unit of replication. All outcomes are simulated from the mechanisms of Table~\ref{tab:mech}.

\subsection{Variance follows leverage; bias does not}
\label{sec:varbias}

\paragraph{Variance.}
The sampling variance of the regression estimator follows $\sigma^2L/n$. Over the 42 cells of the $n$, $d$ and $p$ slices, log RMSE falls with $n$ with slope $-0.50$, rises with $1+d$ with slope $+0.55$ [0.547, 0.556] and falls with $p(1-p)$ with slope $-0.50$ (the predicted slope is $\pm\tfrac12$ in each; Figure~\ref{fig:var} in Appendix~\ref{app:var}). The $d$ slope is therefore not $\tfrac12$ in these data: $(1+d)^{1/2}$ approximates $L^{1/2}$ only roughly, and the slope rests on three degrees ($d=5,20,80$); the intervals are Monte Carlo only and treat the 42 cells as independent although they share graphs and draws. The variance is smallest at $p=\tfrac12$ in all nine mechanism--degree slices that were run (Figure~\ref{fig:bias}, lower row).

\paragraph{Bias.}
The exact population-OLS value of the bias (Eq.~\ref{eq:bias}, evaluated per cell) lies inside the Monte Carlo interval of the measured bias in 82\% of 1283 cells; for mechanism (e) alone it does so in 58\% (largest gap 0.111, cause not diagnosed). The bias is independent of $d$ for the saturating, diffusion and interaction mechanisms (c), (e), (f), and not for the others: the median absolute bias over $p$ and $s$ falls from 0.115 to 0.025 to 0.007 for $d=5,20,80$ in (b), for which the bias reduces to $s[\mathrm{HM}(d_i)/\mathrm{AM}(d_i)-1]$ (Section~\ref{sec:method}), and rises for the threshold mechanism (d) from 0.17 to 0.48 and 0.45. At $p=\tfrac12$, $s=\tfrac12$ the bias of (d) is 0.242, 0.731 and 0.250, non-monotone in $d$; we read this as the observed exposure range straddling the threshold at some degrees and not at others, which we did not test separately. For the saturating mechanism the bias changes sign at $p\approx0.41$--$0.45$, as the curvature term predicts; the bias minimiser over $p$ is not informative for the linear mechanism (the minimum of $|{\rm bias}|$ there is a Monte Carlo artefact and we do not quote it), and the convex mirror (g) has too few $p$ values for the direction of the shift to be tested. \begin{abstract}
Randomised experiments on networks violate the no-interference assumption.
A standard estimator of the global average treatment effect (GATE) regresses the outcome on a unit's own treatment and a function of its neighbours' treatments, then predicts at all-treated and all-control.
We ask how accurate it is, what determines its error, and when it should not be used, treating it as extrapolation from the exposures the experiment produced to the two global corners.
In simulations with exactly known GATE (six interference mechanisms, five synthetic graph families, two Facebook graphs, Bernoulli and cluster designs), the variance follows OLS leverage (RMSE slopes $-0.50$ in $n$, $+0.55$ in $1{+}d$ for mean degree $d$).
The bias is set by the response at the corners, which the data inside the observed exposure range do not identify (our reading, not a separate test): a formula that knows the mechanism matches the realised bias in 82\% of cells, and its dependence on degree differs by mechanism.
Regression beats difference-in-means in 78\% of grid cells at moderate noise (31\% at high noise); the spillover share above which it wins rises with degree (about 0.1, 0.19, 0.38 at $d=5,20,80$), and a threshold mechanism is an exception on synthetic graphs that does not carry over to the real ones.
Two expectations fail: none of the data-computable scores we tried predicts the bias better than a constant, and nominal 95\% intervals cover 74\% of Bernoulli cells, undercovering where bias is large, not where leverage is.
On a sample of cells, flexible learners do not beat the correctly specified regression, except under the threshold mechanism. All outcomes are simulated.
\end{abstract}

\paragraph{Mechanisms and calibration.}
Outcomes are $Y_i=a_i+h_i(z)+\varepsilon_i$ with unit baselines $a_i\sim N(0,1)$ (iid; in some cells correlated with log-degree or community), and $h_i$ one of
(a) $(1{-}s)z_i+sf_i$; (b) $(1{-}s)z_i+s\,c_i/d$; (c) $(1{-}s)z_i+s\,g_{\rm sat}(f_i)$ with $g_{\rm sat}(f)=(1-e^{-3f})/(1-e^{-3})$; (d) $(1{-}s)z_i+s\,\mathbf 1[f_i\ge 0.6]$; (e) $(1{-}s)\sum_{k\le 30}s^k(W^kz)_i$ with $W$ the row-normalised adjacency; (f) $(1{-}s)z_i+\tfrac s2 f_i+\tfrac s2 z_if_i$;
(g) a convex mirror of (c), exploratory. Every mechanism is calibrated to $\gate=1$ with spillover share $s\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75\}$ (fine grid $0.1,\dots,0.9$ at the core cell), and $\gate$ is computed exactly by evaluating $h$ at $\mathbf 1$ and $\mathbf 0$ on each graph draw. Errors are $(\hgate-\gate)/\gate$. Noise $\varepsilon_i$ is iid Gaussian with standard deviation $\sigma$ times the standard deviation of the noise-free outcome ($\sigma\in\{0.25,0.5,1\}$ planned; $\sigma\in\{2,4\}$ added after the freeze and labelled as such). Under Bernoulli assignment DM's bias is $-s\gate$ by construction (measured: $-0.50$ at $s=0.5$; Table~\ref{tab:mech}), and with no noise and the correct specification every error is zero to machine precision.

\paragraph{Estimators and tiers.}
Comparisons are made within an information tier.
\emph{Tier G} (graph known, no mechanism parameter): DM, H\'ajek ($q=0.75,1$), the reporting regression and its ladder (quadratic and spline in $f$, $+$count, $+$two-hop, $+z f$).
\emph{Tier A} (data-adaptive; Bernoulli designs, 14 core and real-graph cells, 200 draws per graph): lasso and ridge on a pool of 15 exposure features with penalty chosen by graph-cluster-fold cross-validation plus a held-out-corner loss in the spirit of \citet{han2023model}; random forest and gradient boosting; and an adaptive-threshold H\'ajek estimator, a simplified version of \citet{thiyageswaran2024data} (threshold from an estimated-MSE rule with a diagonal variance term), reported under that name.
\emph{Tier O} (oracle): the correct feature with the true parameter, and with the parameter fitted by profile least squares for (c), (d), (e).
The score has two parts. For the variance, part (i) is the leverage $L$ of each specification on the ladder (regression, $+$count, $+$two-hop, $+zf$), compared with degree-only predictors of log realised variance. For the bias, part (ii) uses $S$, the root-mean-square over the quadratic, spline, $+$

\paragraph{Release.}
Code, result tables, seeds, data hashes and run times (about 12 CPU-hours on one CPU per run) are in the supplementary archive with a table of which script produces each figure and table.

```console
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

A platform that randomises a feature over its users and compares the groups assumes that one user's outcome does not depend on another's assignment.
On a social or marketplace network this is false, and the quantity of interest is usually the \emph{global average treatment effect} (GATE): the difference in mean outcome if every unit were treated rather than none.
Difference in means (DM) is biased for it; design-based estimators with an exposure mapping \citep{aronow2017estimating,ugander2013graph,eckles2017design} are unbiased only if the mapping is right, and weight the few units whose exposure is extreme.
\emph{Regression adjustment} \citep{chin2019regression,han2023model} avoids both: fit the outcome on the unit's own treatment and graph-based exposure covariates such as the treated fraction of its neighbours, then predict at the all-treated and all-control assignments and difference the predictions.
It uses every unit and needs no weights, which makes it attractive and widely used.

What is not known is how well it works, what governs its error, and when it fails.
The estimator fits a model where exposures occur and evaluates it where they do not: under Bernoulli($p$) assignment a unit with $d$ neighbours sees a treated fraction concentrated around $p$ with spread $\sqrt{p(1-p)/d}$, and the two global corners, fraction $1$ and fraction $0$, lie far outside it.
\citet{chin2019regression} points this out qualitatively and draws the analogy to off-policy evaluation.
We take it as the organising idea, not as a novelty, and ask what it predicts and whether the predictions hold.
Our reading is that the error has two parts with different drivers.
The \emph{variance} is the leverage of the corner contrast in the regression, which grows with degree.
The \emph{bias} is the response's curvature times the raw distance from the observed exposures to the corner, which does not grow with degree for a smooth response, and which no regression can estimate from data that never visit the corner.

We test this on simulated experiments in which the GATE is known exactly, so that each estimator's error, bias and variance are measured and not estimated.
The simulations cross six interference mechanisms (linear, count-based, saturating, threshold, two-hop diffusion, direct$\times$exposure interaction), five synthetic graph families and two real Facebook graphs, Bernoulli and graph-cluster assignment, and DM, H\'ajek exposure estimators, the regression ladder, oracle forms and data-adaptive learners.
The predictions and the acceptance rule for a diagnostic were written down before the runs.

\paragraph{What we find.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em,itemsep=0pt,topsep=2pt]
\item \textbf{Regime map.} Regression beats DM in most cells, and the spillover share above which it wins, $s^\star$, rises with degree (about $0.1$, $0.19$, $0.38$ at $d=5,20,80$ at noise level $\sigma=0.5$) because the variance does. A threshold response is the exception on synthetic graphs at $d\ge 20$, where regression loses at every share, and does not transfer to the two real graphs (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
\item \textbf{Variance and bias differ.} Variance follows leverage with fitted exponents $-0.50$ in $n$ and $+0.55$ in $1{+}d$. Bias is predicted to within Monte-Carlo error in 82\% of cells by a population formula that uses the true response, and depends on degree differently for each mechanism (\S\ref{sec:varbias}).
\item \textbf{Two negative results.} None of the data-computable scores we tried predicts the bias better than a constant, and the usual 95\% interval covers 74\% of Bernoulli cells on average, failing where bias exceeds noise, not where leverage is high (\S\ref{sec:diag}, \S\ref{sec:coverage}).

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{What the results say.}
Regression estimators of the GATE are accurate in this study when the spillover share is large enough that the difference in means is more biased than the regression, which holds in 78\% of the grid at $\sigma=0.5$, and when the response is smooth in exposure. Their variance is predictable from the design and the graph, through the leverage of the corner contrast. Their bias is not: it is set by the response between the observed exposure range and the corners, and the data inside that range do not identify it. Two things we expected to be able to offer practitioners did not work: none of the data-computable scores we tried predicts the bias better than a constant, and the nominal 95\% interval covers the truth in 74\% of Bernoulli cells, mostly because it ignores the bias.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
\emph{Simulated outcomes.} All outcomes come from six mechanisms of our choosing, four of them smooth in exposure, with one baseline model and Gaussian noise; the real graphs supply only structure. The shares of cells in which regression wins are shares of this grid, with the base rate fixed by the cell list, not a population of networks, and the rules for choosing between estimators are evaluated on the same cells on which they were examined. \emph{Graph range.} Synthetic graphs have $n=3000$ (up to $10^4$ in the $n$ slice) and three degrees; the $d$ exponent rests on these three. Thinning real graphs changes clustering and the degree tail together with $d$, so degree effects there are not isolated. The threshold mechanism fails on the synthetic graphs but not on the real ones, and we cannot say why. \emph{Estimators.} Causal message passing needs panel outcomes and graph neural networks were not run; cluster Horvitz--Thompson is not implemented; the adaptive-threshold H\'ajek estimator is a simplified version; the flexible learners are compared at 200 draws per graph with fixed hyperparameters and a restricted feature set. \emph{Design.} Louvain at $\gamma=0.3$ gives a single cluster on the synthetic graphs, so cluster designs are compared at $\gamma=1,3$ and the planted partition only. Mechanism (e) at $s=0.9$ is truncated at $K=30$ steps. $\sigma=2$ and $4$ were added after the freeze. \emph{Theory.} The prediction of the bias is the exact population-OLS value for a known response, and in mechanism (e) it falls outside the Monte Carlo interval in 42\% of cells for a reason we did not diagnose. The leverage identity and the bias of the difference in means are standard; what we add is their joint test across mechanisms, networks and designs.

\paragraph{Implications.}
Three practical readings follow within the scope above. First, report the leverage $L$ and the estimated spillover share alongside the estimate, since both are computable and they carry information about the variance and about whether DM is the better choice. Second, do not read a regression's agreement with richer specifications as evidence that its bias is small: in our cells it is not. Third, do not rely on its default interval when the response may be curved or thresholded. Whether a bias bound that uses only data from the observed exposure range can exist is an open question; our data do not support one for the scores we tried and do not exclude one.

### Review

Review is Forgejo's pull request review: approve, or request changes and say what must change; a comment neither approves nor holds anything. A pull request into `main` of `paper-repo` waits for the owners of the paths it changes, and one into its `release` or `final` waits for the approval of `internal-review-repo`, the only one counted there, of the very commit it merges: a push to it after the approval withdraws it. ### Versions and release

A version for the world's users is a merge of `main` into `release` of `paper-repo`, by a pull request that `internal-review-repo` approved and whose checks pass. The system writes the checks as commit statuses on the pull request's head (`hutian/delivery`, and the world's contract's when it holds one), and a failing one says what is missing and who provides it; nobody else writes a status. Merge with a merge commit, not a squash or a rebase, or the next version conflicts. The system publishes each version as a release of `world/result`, the world's results, with the delivery attached: the users of the world read those releases and nothing else, and every role reads them. The last approval is a merge into `final` in the same way: the system releases the world from it, at once, and nothing pushed after it is part of it. Offer a `release` version as soon as the delivery holds its main work, so that `internal-review-repo`'s review comes while there is still room to act on it; `final` is the last.
